title: 2. What the Company Does: Segments, Revenue Mix & Concrete Examples

epigraph.quote: Our business had exceptional third quarter results, with revenue growth across all four segments, robust bookings and solid operational performance.
epigraph.author: Phebe N. Novakovic, Chairman and CEO, Q3 2026 Earnings Release (October 30, 2026)

web_blocks.title: Four-Segment Revenue, Operating Profit & Real-World Examples

web_blocks.html: General Dynamics operates through four reporting segments: Aerospace, Marine Systems, Combat Systems, and Technologies [1]. In FY2025, consolidated revenue reached $52,550 million (+10.1% YoY) [1][5]. Consolidated operating earnings hit $5,356 million (10.2% margin), after $175 million in corporate expenses [1][5]. Momentum accelerated in the first nine months of 2026. 9M 2026 revenue climbed 10.4% YoY to $42,141 million, up from $38,171 million in 9M 2025 [2][3]. Over the same period, operating earnings rose 12.9% to $4,407 million [2][3]. In Q3 2026 alone, revenue reached $14,566 million (+12.9% YoY) with $1,527 million in operating earnings (10.5% margin) [2][3].

web_blocks.caption: Segment Revenue, Operating Earnings & Margin Mix (FY2025 vs. Q3 2026)
web_blocks.takeaway: *Segment operating profit shares are shown as % of pre-corporate earnings ($5,531M in FY2025; $1,580M in Q3 2026). Marine Systems leads revenue (34.1% in Q3 2026), while Aerospace and Combat Systems deliver the highest margins [1][3].

web_blocks.html: 1. Aerospace (24.9% of FY2025 Revenue; 31.6% of Segment Profit): Anchored by Gulfstream Aerospace (Savannah) and Jet Aviation (Zurich), Aerospace builds and services large-cabin jets [1][6]. Its lineup includes the G700, G800, G650ER, G600, G500, G400, and G280 [1][6]. In 9M 2026, segment revenue climbed to $10,340 million from $9,322 million a year earlier [3]. Operating earnings jumped to $1,516 million from $1,265 million [3]. Concrete End-to-End Example: A corporate or sovereign flight department orders a Gulfstream G700 or G800 (certified April 16, 2025) [6]. Gulfstream collects milestone deposits during the 18-to-36-month build. Workers in Savannah integrate Honeywell engines, Symmetry Flight Deck avionics, and bespoke cabin interiors. Gulfstream delivered its 100th G700 in mid-2026 and placed 34 G800s in service by late 2026 [6]. Post-delivery, Jet Aviation captures recurring MRO, completions, and FBO revenue across its global network, lifting Q3 2026 margin to 14.5% [2][3].

2. Marine Systems (31.8% of FY2025 Revenue; 21.3% of Segment Profit): Marine Systems comprises Electric Boat, Bath Iron Works, and NASSCO [1][7]. In 9M 2026, revenue surged to $13,963 million from $11,905 million a year earlier [3]. Q3 2026 revenue jumped 21.1% YoY to $4,960 million [3]. Concrete End-to-End Example: Electric Boat serves as prime contractor for the Columbia-class ballistic missile submarine (SSBN-826) [7][8]. It also teams with HII's Newport News Shipbuilding on the Virginia-class fast-attack submarine (SSN-774) [7][8]. In Q3 2026, Electric Boat booked $29.5 billion for five Columbia Build II submarines and $42.1 billion for nine Virginia Block VI boats [2][4]. Workers fabricate hull modules in Quonset Point, Rhode Island, then barge them to Groton, Connecticut, for nuclear assembly [3][4]. Meanwhile, Bath Iron Works builds DDG-51 destroyers in Maine, and NASSCO builds T-AO fleet oilers in San Diego [3][4].

3. Combat Systems (17.6% of FY2025 Revenue; 24.1% of Segment Profit): Combat Systems includes Land Systems (GDLS), European Land Systems (GDELS), and Ordnance and Tactical Systems (OTS) [1]. In 9M 2026, revenue rose 3.7% YoY to $6,959 million, though Q3 2026 operating margin contracted 110 basis points YoY to 13.8% (vs. 14.9% in Q3 2025) on program mix (Q3 2026 Form 10-Q) [1][3]. Specifically, U.S. military vehicle revenue fell $203 million in 9M 2026 due to lower U.S. Army recapitalization demand and the termination of the M10 Booker program, and management expects short-term combat vehicle volumes to remain slightly lower (Q3 2026 Form 10-Q). Concrete End-to-End Example: Under NATO's rearmament push, European ministries order Piranha wheeled and ASCOD tracked vehicles from GDELS (+$108 million 9M 2026), while OTS expands 155mm artillery shell production (+$343 million 9M 2026) to offset domestic vehicle softness. Foreign armored-vehicle contracts carry multi-year acceptance milestones, including one deal with $1.2 billion in net unbilled receivables at October 4, 2026 (down from $1.3 billion at year-end 2025) and variable-consideration realization risk (Q3 2026 Form 10-Q, Notes B and E) [1][3].

4. Technologies (25.6% of FY2025 Revenue; 23.1% of Segment Profit): Technologies houses General Dynamics Information Technology (GDIT) and Mission Systems [1]. In 9M 2026, segment revenue grew to $10,879 million from $10,233 million [3]. Q3 2026 revenue rose 10.8% YoY to $3,684 million at a 9.4% operating margin [3]. Concrete End-to-End Example: A U.S. intelligence agency awards GDIT a multi-year IDIQ task order for zero-trust cloud migration and AI cybersecurity. Simultaneously, Mission Systems builds hardened communications, encryption hardware, and fire-control electronics for Virginia- and Columbia-class submarines [1][3].

web_blocks.title: Customer Concentration, Aftermarket Annuity & Unfunded Backlog Risk

web_blocks.html: Geographic & Customer Concentration Across Segments: Per Q3 2026 Form 10-Q Note B, total U.S. government revenue reached $10,007 million (68.7% of $14,566 million Q3 sales)—comprising $8,534 million Department of War (58.6%), $1,276 million Non-DoW federal agencies (8.8%, concentrated almost entirely in Technologies at $1,262 million), and $197 million Foreign Military Sales (1.4%). At the segment level, Marine Systems is 99.96% U.S. government ($4,958 million of $4,960 million) and Technologies is 95.1% U.S. government ($3,504 million of $3,684 million). Commercial and international buyers account for the remaining 31.3%, led by Aerospace ($1,454 million U.S. commercial; $1,780 million non-U.S. commercial in Q3 2026) and Combat Systems ($828 million non-U.S. government). That heavy sovereign dependence ties defense backlog conversion directly to Congressional appropriations: Congress missed the October 1, 2026 start of federal FY2027 and enacted a Continuing Resolution (CR) on September 2, 2026 running through December 11, 2026 (Q3 2026 Form 10-Q).

Aftermarket Services & Recurring Annuity Base: Aftermarket support provides an underappreciated earnings stabilizer across Aerospace and Defense [1][11]. Gulfstream and Jet Aviation run a global MRO network across North America, Europe, and Asia [6][12]. That network generates recurring parts and inspection revenue tied to flight hours rather than new-jet deliveries [6][12]. Similarly, Marine Systems performs submarine overhauls and lifecycle engineering at Groton and Norfolk, producing steady cost-plus cash flows between hull deliveries [7][11].

Cross-Segment Backlog Resilience & Unfunded Concentration: The $220,339 million ($220.3 billion) Q3 2026 backlog spans Navy submarine blocks, Gulfstream deposits, European armor orders, and GDIT task orders, alongside $50,330 million of unfunded IDIQ/option potential ($270.7 billion total estimated contract value) (Q3 2026 Form 10-Q) [12]. Crucially, however, $108,543 million (49.3% of total backlog) is unfunded—up sharply from $32,387 million at Q2 2026—because Marine Systems unfunded backlog jumped from $22,826 million to $99,576 million following the Columbia Build II and Virginia Block VI awards. While funded backlog sits at $111,796 million ($47,289 million in Marine Systems, $24,460 million in Aerospace), conversion of the $99.6 billion unfunded shipyard backlog depends on multi-year Congressional defense appropriations beyond the current CR expiring December 11, 2026 (Q3 2026 Form 10-Q).

book_paragraphs: When you and I look at General Dynamics on a single-page financial summary, it is easy to lump it in with generic defense primes. That would be a mistake. General Dynamics is actually a four-cylinder machine where no single segment accounts for more than 35% of revenue, yet each cylinder plays a distinct economic role in the portfolio.

Start with the profit engine: Aerospace. Generating $13.11 billion in FY2025 revenue and $1,746 million in operating earnings—a 13.3% margin that expanded to 14.5% in Q3 2026—Aerospace is where Gulfstream and Jet Aviation live. Picture a Fortune 100 board or a sovereign ministry ordering a Gulfstream G700 or G800. You are not buying a commodity airframe; you are buying a bespoke, ultra-long-range flying office certified by the FAA and EASA. Gulfstream collects milestone deposits while the jet is built in Savannah, hands over the keys—having crossed its 100th G700 delivery in mid-2026 and placed 34 G800s into service by late 2026—and then Jet Aviation services that aircraft for the next twenty years across its global MRO and FBO network.

Now contrast that with the growth engine: Marine Systems. At $16.72 billion in FY2025 revenue and $4.96 billion in Q3 2026 alone (up 21.1% year-over-year), Marine Systems is the largest top-line contributor, yet its 7.0% to 7.9% operating margin looks deceptively modest. Why? Because building nuclear submarines is the most complex industrial undertaking on earth. Electric Boat is the prime contractor for the Columbia-class ballistic missile submarine—the crown jewel of the U.S. nuclear triad—and co-builds the Virginia-class attack submarine. Think about the physical choreography: hull sections are fabricated at Quonset Point, Rhode Island, barged to Groton, Connecticut, and welded into nuclear-powered leviathans. In the third quarter of 2026 alone, the U.S. Navy finalized $29.5 billion for five Columbia Build II boats and $42.1 billion for nine Virginia Block VI boats. Meanwhile, Bath Iron Works builds Arleigh Burke destroyers in Maine, and NASSCO builds fleet oilers in San Diego.

The third cylinder, Combat Systems, generated $9.25 billion in FY2025 revenue at a 14.4% margin, though Q3 2026 exposed an important mix shift beneath the surface. While 9M 2026 revenue grew 3.7% to $6,959 million on surging 155mm artillery munitions (+$343 million) and European armored vehicles (+$108 million), U.S. military vehicle revenue contracted by $203 million following lower Army recapitalization demand and the termination of the M10 Booker light-tank program. That mix shift trimmed Q3 2026 Combat Systems margins by 110 basis points to 13.8%, and management cautioned that near-term combat vehicle volumes will dip slightly—alongside $1.2 billion in net unbilled receivables on a single international tracked-vehicle contract that we will audit in Chapter 6.

Finally, Technologies—housing GDIT and Mission Systems—generated $13.47 billion in FY2025 revenue at a 9.5% operating margin, and grew 10.8% in Q3 2026 to $3.68 billion. It is asset-light, people-intensive, and embedded inside federal cloud modernization, cybersecurity, and submarine combat electronics. Together, these four segments give you a rare blend: commercial luxury aviation margins, sovereign nuclear-deterrent backlog, NATO land-warfare hardware, and recurring federal IT cash flows.

Before we move to unit economics, pause and appreciate how well those four cylinders balance one another. When commercial aviation slowed in 2020, defense segments carried the cash flow. When defense margins compressed under supply-chain friction in 2024–2025, Gulfstream's G700 and G800 ramp stepped up to drive consolidated operating earnings higher.

To make sure these four segments do not blur together as accounting lines, step back and picture the customer diversity across them. On Monday morning, a Gulfstream sales executive in Savannah is negotiating a $75 million G700 completion specification with a Fortune 100 flight department—a pure commercial, milestone-billed transaction driven by cabin acoustics, range from New York to Tokyo, and dispatch reliability. On Tuesday afternoon, an Electric Boat program manager in Groton is reviewing cost-plus-incentive-fee labor hours with Naval Sea Systems Command for a Columbia-class ballistic missile submarine that will patrol the Pacific into the 2080s.

On Wednesday, a General Dynamics European Land Systems engineer in Madrid or Vienna is qualifying a Piranha 8x8 armored vehicle for a NATO ministry of defense under multi-year production terms. And on Thursday, a GDIT cloud architect in Falls Church is migrating classified healthcare or intelligence workloads onto sovereign cloud infrastructure under a task-order contract. Four completely different buyers, four distinct contract structures, all sitting under one $52.55 billion roof.

One detail that casual investors often miss in Chapter 2 is how much recurring service revenue sits quietly inside Aerospace and Marine Systems. Every time a Gulfstream G650, G700, or G800 logs 500 flight hours, it enters a scheduled maintenance window at a Gulfstream or Jet Aviation service center for avionics checks, engine support, and cabin refurbishment. That aftermarket stream carries higher margins and far lower cyclicality than new-jet deliveries.

The same dynamic holds in Marine Systems: once a Virginia-class submarine enters the fleet, Electric Boat performs ongoing lifecycle engineering, modernization, and overhaul work for decades. So even when a new hull delivery slips by a quarter, the installed base keeps generating steady, predictable revenue.

Notice how those four segments balance each other across different macroeconomic regimes. When interest rates rise or corporate C-suites pause jet orders, the U.S. Navy and NATO allies keep funding submarines, tanks, and artillery. When defense budgets face continuing resolutions in Washington, Gulfstream's global ultra-high-net-worth and corporate buyers keep Savannah's completion hangars humming. That natural diversification inside one enterprise is a major reason GD's earnings volatility has remained remarkably low.

As you walk through the rest of this monograph, keep those four real-world customer stories in mind—from the Savannah completion hangar to the Groton submarine dry dock—because every revenue and margin figure in our financial tables traces directly back to them.

Every time you hear an earnings headline about Gulfstream deliveries or Navy submarine awards, come back to these four operational vignettes—they explain how a $52.55 billion industrial enterprise actually generates its cash, and why investors must distinguish between funded backlog ($111.8 billion) and unfunded submarine backlog ($108.5 billion total, $99.6 billion in Marine Systems) when Washington operates under continuing resolutions.

One critical blind spot in a casual segment overview is customer concentration and budget-timing exposure. In Q3 2026, U.S. government buyers accounted for $10,007 million, or 68.7% of consolidated revenue—and an astonishing 99.96% of Marine Systems ($4,958 million of $4,960 million) and 95.1% of Technologies ($3,504 million of $3,684 million, including $1,262 million from non-defense agencies). Because Congress missed the October 1, 2026 fiscal-year deadline and is operating under a Continuing Resolution through December 11, 2026, converting GD's newly booked $99.6 billion of unfunded Marine Systems backlog into multi-year cash depends directly on future defense appropriations.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: Look closely at the profit-versus-revenue split: Aerospace and Combat Systems together represent only 42.5% of FY2025 revenue, yet they generate 55.7% of segment operating profit. Marine Systems represents 31.8% of revenue and will drive the bulk of top-line growth through 2030, so even a 100-basis-point margin recovery at Electric Boat moves the consolidated earnings needle dramatically.
